You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Make her close her jacket fully
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Compared with the input image, is there visible progress toward closing the woman's jacket, no visible progress, or is progress indeterminate?
node.criteria: Pass: comparable visible evidence of the same jacket closure region in both images establishes a change toward closing, while the edited jacket is not fully closed. Fail: the same relevant closure region is sufficiently visible and comparable in both images, and establishes no change toward closing. Unknown: the closure region is obscured, not comparable, or the direction of change cannot be established. Do not treat a pose change, occlusion, or lack of visibility as evidence of no progress.
node.binding: Compare only visible evidence of the same woman's jacket closure region in source and edit. The source shows the jacket front; the edited pose and drape may obscure it, in which case progress is unknown rather than absent.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image shows a changed pose and drape that obscure the jacket’s closure region, so the same region cannot be compared reliably with the source to establish progress toward closing.

fulfillment: The unresolved result is driven by the progress check, not a transport or schema failure: both dependencies executed validly, and the edited image clearly fails the fully-closed endpoint. The source shows the jacket front hanging open; in the edit, the changed pose and swinging drape obscure the closure area, so the images do not reliably establish whether any requested closure progress occurred. Keep the endpoint check strict, but refine the progress criterion to compare only visible, corresponding jacket-closure evidence and return unknown when pose or occlusion prevents that comparison; do not treat unrelated pose changes as progress or infer absence of progress from low confidence. The reference label is aggregate guidance, not proof that the edit made progress, so do not force a positive label or weaken the rubric to match it.
